content: The stinging nettle, scientifically known as Urtica dioica, is a herbaceous flowering plant that is native to Europe, Asia, northern Africa, and North America. It is the most well-known species within the genus Urtica. This plant is characterized by its stinging hairs, known as trichomes, which act as a defense mechanism. When touched, the tips of these hairs break off, transforming them into needle-like structures that inject a mixture of chemicals, including acetylcholine, histamine, serotonin (5-HT), and possibly formic acid. This chemical cocktail causes a stinging sensation or paresthesia, which is the origin of the plant's common name. It is also colloquially referred to as the 7-minute itch. The taxonomy of stinging nettles has been historically complex, with older sources using various systematic names. While more species were previously recognized, current classifications identify at least five subspecies: 1. U. dioica subsp. dioica (European stinging nettle) – Found in Europe, Asia, and northern Africa. 2. U. dioica subsp. afghanica – Found in southwestern and central Asia, including Iran. 3. U. dioica subsp. gansuensis – Found in eastern Asia, particularly China. 4. U. dioica subsp. gracilis (American stinging nettle) – Found in North America. 5. U. dioica subsp. holosericea (hairy nettle) – Found in North America. Several other names, such as U. breweri, U. californica, and U. cardiophylla, were once considered distinct species but are now regarded as synonyms of U. dioica. The plant is also known by various vernacular names, including tall nettle, slender nettle, California nettle, burning weed, and bull nettle. Stinging nettle is a perennial plant that grows to a height of 1–2 meters during the summer and dies back to the ground in winter. It has distinctive yellow, spreading roots and soft green leaves that are 3–15 cm long, with serrated edges, a heart-shaped base, and a pointed tip. The plant thrives in northern Europe and much of Asia, particularly in moist soil. It is less common in southern Europe and northern Africa due to its preference for moist environments. In North America, it is widely distributed across Canada, the United States (except Hawaii), and northern Mexico, though it is less abundant than in northern Europe. The European subspecies has been introduced to both North and South America. In the United Kingdom, stinging nettles are often associated with human habitation and abandoned buildings. Their presence may indicate elevated levels of phosphate and nitrogen in the soil, often due to human or animal waste. This phenomenon is particularly evident in Scotland, where nettles can mark the sites of long-abandoned crofts from the Highland Clearances. Medicinal Uses Stinging nettle has been used in herbal medicine for centuries, with records of its use dating back to ancient Greece. In Germany, nettle leaf is traditionally used as an adjuvant treatment for arthritis. Extracts from nettle leaves contain bioactive compounds that reduce levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and other pro-inflammatory cytokines. Research has demonstrated that nettle leaf extract inhibits the genetic transcription factor NF-κB, which activates TNF-α and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) in the synovial tissue of joints. A study on healthy volunteers showed that nettle extract significantly reduced TNF-α and IL-1β concentrations in response to pro-inflammatory stimulation. Another study involving 40 patients with acute arthritis compared the effects of 200 mg of diclofenac (an anti-inflammatory drug) to 50 mg of the same drug combined with stewed nettle leaf. Both groups experienced a 70% improvement in joint scores, but the addition of nettle extract allowed for a 75% reduction in the diclofenac dose while maintaining the same anti-inflammatory benefits and reducing side effects. This suggests that nettle extract may enable lower doses of COX-2 inhibitors, potentially mitigating their adverse effects, such as elevated TNF-α and IL-1β levels. Nettle root extract, distinct from the leaf extract, is used to alleviate symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Cooking, crushing, or chopping stinging nettle leaves neutralizes their stinging hairs. The leaves are nutrient-rich, containing high levels of calcium and iron, and can be used to make soups or teas. However, due to their high nitrate content, which can convert to carcinogenic nitrosamines in the digestive tract, nettle leaves should not be used in baby food. Anti-Itch Treatment If stung by a nettle, effective treatments include creams containing antihistamines or hydrocortisone. Folk remedies for alleviating the itching include: Applying juice from crushed dock leaves (Rumex spp.), which often grow near nettles. Using juice from jewelweed (Impatiens capensis or Impatiens pallida). Rubbing the underside of a fern leaf (containing spore pods) on the affected area. Applying mud to the sting, allowing it to dry, and then brushing it off. Washing the area quickly with water. Applying ice to reduce itchiness. Moistening the area with saliva. Using a paste made from baking soda and water, which may neutralize the formic acid released by the nettle's hairs. Influence on Language and Culture In Great Britain, the stinging nettle is the only common stinging plant and has influenced several English idioms. To nettle someone means to irritate or annoy them. The phrase to grasp the nettle originates from Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1 and means to confront a problem directly. This metaphor refers to the fact that firmly grasping a nettle crushes its stinging hairs, reducing the likelihood of being stung. Interestingly, nettle stings have been used as a folk remedy for rheumatism, as the initial stinging sensation transitions to a warming effect that may alleviate pain. In German, the idiom im Nesseln gesetzen (to sit in nettles) means to find oneself in trouble or a difficult situation. Edibility When cooked, stinging nettle has a flavor similar to spinach and is rich in vitamins A, C, and D, as well as iron, potassium, manganese, and calcium. Native Americans harvested young nettle plants in the spring as a vegetable when other food sources were scarce. In Scandinavia, nettle soup made from young shoots is considered a seasonal delicacy. Cooking or drying the plant neutralizes its toxic components. However, stinging nettle should not be consumed after it begins flowering and setting seeds, as the leaves develop cystoliths—gritty particles that can irritate the urinary tract. Additional Uses The stems of stinging nettle contain bast fibers, which have historically been used as a textile material, similar to linen. These fibers are extracted through a retting process.
